newsitem.title: FRANCE: France hikes company taxes to meet EMU goal.
newsitem.headline: France hikes company taxes to meet EMU goal.

text.p: France's leftist government raised taxes on big business Monday to bring down this year's public deficit after an audit found the shortfall running well above the level required to qualify for a single European currency.

The audit, ordered by Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin after he took office last month, showed the 1997 deficit running at 3.5 to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product, significantly beyond the 3 percent limit set by the Maastricht Treaty for entry into European monetary union.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said that to meet the target, the government would cut the deficit by 32 billion francs ($5.3 billion) -- with 22 billion ($3.6 billion) in higher taxes on companies' profits and capital gains and 10 billion ($1.7 billion) in spending cuts.

The measures won endorsement from Germany, France's chief partner in the drive to launch economic and monetary union in 1999. German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the French were doing their best to meet the Maastricht target.

Strauss-Kahn, who telephoned Waigel before announcing his measures, refused to set a numerical deficit target for 1997, the reference year to qualify for economic and monetary union, but said the measures "concern 0.4 percent of GDP."
"Less would have been insufficient, more would have blocked economic growth," he told a news conference.
France would meet the Maastricht criteria "in the same conditions as its (European Union) partners," he said.
Economists said the measures announced should bring down the 1997 deficit to about 3.2 percent of GDP, sufficient to qualify for the new single currency, to be called the euro.
In line with Jospin's pledge that there would be "no new austerity plan" to qualify for EMU, the package contained no tax increase on households.
The defence budget will bear two billion francs ($331 million) of this year's 10 billion ($1.7 billion) spending cuts.

Arguing that company profits were at a record high and that previous centre-right governments had given industry tax breaks and subsidies, Strauss-Kahn announced a 15 percent increase in company tax in 1997 and 1998, falling to 10 percent in 1999.
The increases are calculated on the 33.3 percent basic rate of company tax. Since 1995, there has been a 10 percent surtax and the rate stands currently at 36.6 percent.
Corporate capital gains will be taxed at the same rate as profits.
Small firms were exempted from the increase.

The government said it was facing a tax shortfall this year of 15 billion to 17 billion francs ($2.5 billion to $2.8 billion) and a public spending overshoot of 12 billion to 20 billion francs ($2 billion and $3.3 billion).

In addition, the welfare deficit in the main social security fund was running at 35 billion to 38 billion francs ($5.8 billion and $6.3 billion), compared with the 30.4 billion francs ($5 billion) target initially forecast.
Economists said the tax package was slightly bigger than expected but its concentration on big business was predictable.

"It is the corporate sector that takes the pain. The overall impact is slightly larger than people had been expecting. All this is wholly coherent with the extremely Keynesian approach of the government," said Christopher Potts, an economist at Paris brokers Cheuvreux de Virieu.
The centre-right opposition, ousted from government in a June 1 parliamentary election upset, attacked the government's emphasis on taxing business rather than cutting spending.
